about: A toolkit programmers use to build reliable apps in TypeScript, a popular programming language.

prs.title: Settings that refer to other settings now fill in correctly
prs.broken: In a settings file, one setting can use another. The toolkit read the filled-in text again, so it could turn into a different, missing setting. A line that used itself, like extending PATH, crashed the app.
prs.changed: Each setting is now filled in once, and the text that was filled in is never read again.
prs.matters: Settings come out the way the file says, and a common PATH line no longer crashes the app.

prs.title: Live updates no longer lose text after a carriage return
prs.broken: Servers built with the toolkit can push live updates to a browser. Text with a lone carriage return, which progress bars use, was sent as one line, so the browser lost everything after the first return.
prs.changed: Every kind of line break now starts a new line in the update, the way the format expects.
prs.matters: Progress output and other text reach the browser whole.

prs.title: Reading a stream in chunks no longer loses an item
prs.broken: A common way to split a stream of data, for example a file's header from its body, read one item too far and threw it away. Every chunk after the first lost its first item.
prs.changed: The split now stops right at the item that ends the chunk, so the next chunk starts with the right one.
prs.matters: Programs that split data this way get all of it, not most of it.

prs.title: Adding hours now works across clock changes
prs.broken: Adding hours or minutes to a time was done on the clock face. On the nights clocks go back or forward, adding one minute could jump back almost an hour, and adding 24 hours gave only 23.
prs.changed: Hours, minutes and seconds are now added as real time passed, while days, months and years still follow the calendar.
prs.matters: Timers and schedules built with the toolkit stay right on the two nights a year the clocks change.

prs.title: Uploads with long or odd file names no longer fail
prs.broken: A web server built with the toolkit saves each uploaded file under its own name. A long Chinese or Japanese name, or a name of just '.' or '..', made the whole upload fail with a server error.
prs.changed: Long names are now cut to fit the disk's real limit, keeping the extension, and '.' and '..' are saved under a safe name.
prs.matters: People can upload files named in any language, and an odd name can't break the upload.

prs.title: Data files saved on Windows now read correctly on Node
prs.broken: Some Windows tools put an invisible mark at the start of a file. Data sent with that mark was rejected by apps running on Node, while the same app on other platforms read it fine.
prs.changed: Node now drops the invisible mark when it reads text, the same way the other platforms already did.
prs.matters: An app gives the same answer wherever it runs, and files from Windows tools just work.

prs.title: Monitoring no longer repeats old lowest and highest values
prs.broken: When an app sent timing reports in intervals, each report claimed the smallest and largest values since startup, not for that interval. Dashboards showed values that never happened then.
prs.changed: After the first report, I leave those two values out, as the project's other reporting tool already does.
prs.matters: Charts for each time window show only what actually happened in that window.

prs.title: Speed reports now count every slow request
prs.broken: Apps can report how long things take, sorted into ranges like 'under 10 ms'. With custom ranges, anything above the top range went uncounted; with built-in ranges, the top range appeared twice.
prs.changed: I made all three reporting tools handle both kinds of range lists the same, correct way.
prs.matters: Dashboards built on these reports show true numbers again, such as the typical response time.

prs.title: An AI's 'thinking' now arrives in one piece, not hundreds
prs.broken: With Ollama (which runs AI models on your own computer), a model's thinking came back chopped into hundreds of pieces, one per word, and its answer started before it finished thinking.
prs.changed: I made the library ignore the empty answer text Ollama sends along with each bit of thinking.
prs.matters: Chat apps built on it keep a clean history and show thinking and answers in the right order.

prs.title: Overlapping groups of items no longer lose items at the end
prs.broken: A tool that splits a list into overlapping groups (like 1-2-3, then 3-4-5) dropped items from the last, shorter group: 5 and 6 came out as just 6.
prs.changed: The last group now keeps all its items, matching what the library's older version did.
prs.matters: Programs that process data in overlapping windows no longer quietly lose data at the end.

prs.title: Settings with '=' in their value are no longer cut short
prs.broken: Settings written as name=value pairs lost everything after a second '=' sign. A login key for a monitoring service lost its ending, so the service refused the app's data.
prs.changed: I split each pair at the first '=' only, so the rest of the value stays intact.
prs.matters: Apps can send their performance data to monitoring services that require a login.

prs.title: Forms that send a single item in a list now work
prs.broken: If a form field could hold a list, like tags, and only one item was sent, the server rejected the request with an error. Two or more items worked.
prs.changed: The server now accepts a single item and treats it as a list of one.
prs.matters: The library's own sending and receiving sides now agree, so these requests stop failing.

prs.title: Data streams no longer freeze when one part stops early
prs.broken: A program can split a stream of data into groups and read each one separately. If one reader stopped early, the whole program froze once that group's backlog filled up.
prs.changed: When a reader finishes, its group is now closed, so extra items for it are dropped instead of piling up.
prs.matters: Programs that only need part of the data no longer hang forever.

prs.title: Multi-line text in settings files keeps the right ending
prs.broken: YAML is a common format for settings files. When reading a block of multi-line text from one, the library added or dropped line breaks at the end, against the format's official rules.
prs.changed: I made it follow the official rules for line breaks at the end of a block, with tests for each case.
prs.matters: Text read from settings files now comes out exactly as the file says.

prs.title: Windows-saved settings files no longer get a stray line break
prs.broken: TOML is another settings-file format. In files saved on Windows, every multi-line text value started with an extra line break that shouldn't be there.
prs.changed: I made the reader skip the Windows-style line break too, as it already did for the usual one.
prs.matters: The same settings file now gives the same result no matter which computer saved it.
